chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Ziyad ibn Suqah, from al-Hakam ibn 'Utaybah, who said:
I said to Abi Ja'far عليه السلام: Some people have thirty-two teeth in their mouths, while some of them have twenty-eight teeth. According to how many is the blood-money for the teeth apportioned?

He said: 'The natural formation is only twenty-eight teeth: twelve in the front of the mouth and sixteen in its back. On this basis the blood-money of the teeth was apportioned. The compensation for each of the front teeth, if it is broken until it is lost, is five hundred dirhams, and they are twelve teeth, making six thousand dirhams. For each of the back teeth there are two hundred and fifty dirhams, and they are sixteen teeth, so their compensation is four thousand dirhams. Thus the total blood-money of the front and back teeth is ten thousand dirhams. The blood-money was only established on this basis, so whatever exceeds twenty-eight teeth has no blood-money, and whatever is lacking has no blood-money. Thus we found it in the Book of 'Ali عليه السلام.'

He said: Then al-Hakam ibn 'Utaybah said: I said, blood-monies were only taken before today from camels, cattle, and sheep. He said: 'That was only in the desert regions before Islam. Then when Islam became manifest and silver currency became abundant among the people, Amir al-Mu'minin عليه السلام apportioned it in silver.'

Al-Hakam said: I said to him, what do you think about those who today are among the people of the desert regions—what is taken from them today in blood-money: camels or silver? He said: 'Camels today are equivalent to silver; rather, they are better than silver in blood-money. They used to take from them in accidental blood-money one hundred camels, reckoning each camel at one hundred dirhams, and that is ten thousand.' I said to him: Then what are the ages of the one hundred camels? He said: 'Those upon which a full year has passed, all of them males.'

key_terms.الْأَسْنَانِ: the teeth for which compensation is being legally apportioned
key_terms.الْإِبِلِ: camels used as a basis of dīyah valuation
key_terms.الْمَقَادِيمِ: the front teeth at the front of the mouth
key_terms.الْمَوَاخِيرِ: the back teeth in the rear of the mouth
key_terms.دِرْهَمٍ: silver dirham used as the monetary measure of compensation
key_terms.دِيَةُ: blood-money or legal financial compensation for bodily injury

ai.seo_question: How is the dīyah for teeth calculated in Shia hadith, and is it valued in camels or silver?
ai.summary: This hadith sets out the legal apportionment of the dīyah for teeth based on a natural count of twenty-eight teeth, distinguishing between front and back teeth and assigning fixed dirham values to each. It also explains the valuation of dīyah in silver and camels, attributing the monetary apportionment to Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام.
